text:
In late August 1854, cholera arrived in Soho, a crowded, poor district of London. Within ten days, more than five hundred people living near Broad Street had died. Entire families were wiped out. Shops closed. Those who could afford to leave fled the neighborhood, and the dead were carried away in carts faster than the parish could record their names.

Cholera was no stranger to Britain. It causes violent diarrhea and vomiting that drain the body of water, and a victim can go from healthy to dead in a day. Earlier epidemics in the 1830s and 1840s had killed tens of thousands. Yet nobody agreed on what caused it. The dominant belief, held by most physicians and officials, was the miasma theory, which said that disease spread through foul air rising from rotting waste, sewers and marshes. The smell of London, which was considerable, seemed to prove the point.

John Snow, a physician living a short walk from Broad Street, doubted this. Snow had made his name by pioneering the careful use of anesthesia, and he had given chloroform to Queen Victoria during childbirth. He was a teetotaler and a vegetarian, quiet and methodical, and he trusted measurement over tradition. Years earlier, during the epidemic of 1848 and 1849, he had reasoned that cholera must be swallowed rather than breathed. The illness attacked the gut first, not the lungs. Whatever caused it, he argued, passed from the bowels of the sick into the mouths of the healthy, most likely through contaminated water. In 1849 he published a short pamphlet making that case. Few took it seriously.

The Broad Street outbreak gave him a chance to prove it. Snow began by walking the streets and knocking on doors. He wanted to know where each victim had lived and, above all, what they had drunk. He obtained the official list of deaths from the registrar and marked each address on a map of the district. A pattern emerged. The deaths clustered tightly around one spot, the public water pump on Broad Street, where residents drew water for cooking and drinking.

The pattern was not perfect, and Snow treated the exceptions as seriously as the rule. Near the pump stood a workhouse housing more than five hundred people, yet only a handful died. Snow found that the workhouse had its own well. A brewery on nearby Broad Street also escaped almost untouched. Its workers were given free beer and, it seems, rarely drank from the pump. On the other side, he heard of a widow living far away in Hampstead who died of cholera. Her family told him that she had liked the taste of the Broad Street water so much that she had a bottle of it carted to her home each day. A niece who drank the same water also fell ill and died. These cases, the quiet ones and the strange ones, fit his theory better than any smell in the air could.

On the evening of 7 September, Snow went to the local board of guardians, the men responsible for the parish, and laid out his evidence. He asked them to take the handle off the pump. They agreed. Without the handle, nobody could draw water, and the pump stood silent. Snow's detractors later noted that the epidemic had already been fading by then, since many residents had fled and the number of new cases was falling. Snow acknowledged this himself. But he believed the removal of the handle had still saved lives, and the symbolism was enormous. A single act, based on evidence rather than fear, had been taken against the disease.

The story did not end there. A local curate named Henry Whitehead, who at first scorned Snow's idea, set out to disprove it. He knew the neighborhood and its people far better than Snow did. The more he investigated, the more he came around. Whitehead eventually uncovered the likely source. A baby living at 40 Broad Street had died of diarrhea days before the outbreak exploded. Her mother had washed the soiled nappies in a bucket and emptied the water into a cesspool a few feet from the pump's well. Inspection later showed that the cesspool's brickwork was decayed and leaking, so waste could seep into the water supply. Snow and Whitehead had found their trail from one sick child to hundreds of deaths.

Authorities were slow to accept the conclusion. An official inquiry reviewed the case and decided the evidence was not convincing enough, and the miasma theory remained the favorite for years. Snow died in 1858, aged forty-five, still unsure whether the world would ever believe him.

It did, in time. Within a generation, microscopes and the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch confirmed that living germs, in this case a bacterium, caused cholera and spread through water. Cities built sewers and clean supplies. Snow's map, and his habit of asking where, when and among whom a disease strikes, became the foundation of modern epidemiology. He had solved the mystery with a notebook, a map and stubborn curiosity.
